messages.content:
A Witcher Story

The story follows Geralt on one of his contracts. He was called to a small (6-8 house maybe) village after all inhabitants had just fled due to something killing the people. The village sat in a secluded area surrounded with empty fields on one side and lush forest on the other. One or two people going missing or being found dead wasn’t a cause for suspicion in these conditions and in this time (monsters, beasts, war, etc.). However, the day after two villagers turned up dead from a supposed wolf attach in the woods, the town herbalist and a farmer are found mutilated in a clearing. There were obvious signs of a struggle, and the scene was a gruesome sight. This was not a wolf or even a bear that caused this. Trees were smashed. The earth was dug up. The bodies had wounds so terrible that any that laid eyes upon them gave their life to drink and contributed to society no more. With no way to defend themselves the rest of the village fled their home. One villager (maybe Arthur) met Geralt in a pub in a neighboring town and hired him to stake out the village. It was difficult to find housing that was not burned to a crisp or had an axe taken to it in this time of war. Even the smallest rumor of Temerian loyalty was excuse enough for Nilgardian soldiers to have their fun. The villager explained that some of the escapees were struggling. After failing to find new homes, they had become beggars, thieves, and whores. The villager held hopes that Geralt may be able to find out what was haunting his home and kill it so he and his family may be able to return and live in peace. Geralt accepted the contract.

Geralt arrived at the village and while inspecting the abandoned houses he found one was not abandoned. The door was open. There was a young woman inside, sitting at a table clutching what looked like a dirty bit of straw clothing. Perhaps a hat. She seemed not even to notice him as he entered. She just stared at the opposite wall of the house, absently rubbing the straw thing between her fingers. Geralt quickly scanned the rest of the one room house. One large bed against the far wall. Fresh grain, cabbages, and potatoes in the pantry. Drying herbs hung from the ceiling. Farming tools were propped up against the wall near the door. This must be the dead farmer’s house. And this must be the dead farmers wife.

Geralt stepped fully into the house and a cleared his throat awkwardly. The woman did not move but continued to clutch the straw thing. Probably the farmer’s hat. This situation was going nowhere fast, and Geralt decided that as usual the direct approach was needed.

“Is that his hat? Your husband’s?” He said as he took a seat at the table across from the woman. “He’s the farmer they found, right?”

For the first time the woman seemed to notice him. She slowly brought her gaze from the wall to his with a look of confusion. Looking him up and down she spoke in a rough, pained voice as though it hadn’t been used in days, “Who are you? You aren’t from here. Why are you here?” A look of anger crossed her face. “They sent you, didn’t they? They couldn’t convince me to come with them, so they hired some sword to force me to. Well, you aren’t taking me. I’ll tell you what I told them and then you can leave. I am going to live out the rest of my days in this house whether I live to eighty or die tomorrow from that demon that killed Willem. When I leave this village, it will be in a casket.” She spat out the last words like venom, clutching the ratty straw bit so tightly her knuckles whitened.

Geralt tried to smile gently. “I swear to you I am no sell-sword, and I am not here to take you anywhere. I am a witcher. And I can promise you it is not in my code to kidnap grieving widows.”

The woman frowned and furrowed her brow. “A witcher…” She whispered to herself. “Good to know someone is taking this seriously. But I can’t help you. I’m sorry. I don’t know any more than you do. I couldn’t even bring myself to go out and identify -.” She grimaced and sighed. “Arthur had to do it.”

“Fine. I’ve already gotten descriptions. If you could point me in the direction of the scene, you won’t hear from me again.” Geralt hesitated. He didn’t know why he kept trying to give humans advice when the only thanks got was a beer in the face or moldy tomato juice down his trousers. “But… you should leave. For a few days. After I’m done here then you and the whole village can come back.”

The woman said nothing but stared straight into his face. She did not blink, and her frown deepened. There was nothing in her eyes except a cold emptiness and rage.

It was difficult to intimidate Geralt. He had seen many horrors throughout his life, and he was often the most intimidating person in the room anyway. However, he recognized this stare and felt a small shiver run down his spine. This woman would not be afraid to kill a man.

She could not kill Geralt, of course, but that didn’t mean she wouldn’t try. She was a grieving widow with nothing to lose. Geralt decided to make a hasty exit before any events transpired. At least there weren’t any tomatoes in the house.

Well, that turned out to be a dead end, but Geralt never intended to find that woman anyway. He gained nothing and lost only time. He did his best to help her which is all he was obliged to do. Whatever comes of her now will be a result of her own actions.



Summary
The woman (Lyra maybe as a name?) turns out to be hundreds (??) of years old possessed by a Mist Wraith. This is the only type of wraith that can possess people. Very rare at this level. The husband put it together that every time she left the village for some reason or other was when the murders happened. The herbalist, really a witch or maybe sorceress (are they the same?) was in disguise and found out. Maybe she was secretly researching the murders and found out what husband knew somehow? Maybe husband only thought wife was murderer and not something paranormal until sorceress found him and talked with him secretly. Did Sorceress think Lyra was a Mist Wraith right away or did she think her another creature by mistake? Neither knew that the Mist Wraith had been possessing Lyra for so long and had grown so strong. Either Lyra tricks husband (Willem) and lures him and herbalist (sorceress Elara) to the clearing in the woods or the other way around. I think Lyra finds out they are plotting and tricks them. Geralt goes to the clearing and finds bodies. Don’t think he knows it’s a mist Wraith yet but he knows something is wrong. Maybe he thinks it is something else first? Has to go back to Lyra to ask more questions about village people. Finds out she’s been having fainting spells. Remembers she was staring into space. Begins to suspect a budding Mist Wraith. Asks Lyra if she’s ever woken up in weird places holding weird trinkets, etc. He is trying to find Mist Wraith’s body and artifact. It probably tried to hide them when it possessed her. She said something about the mine (maybe?). Geralt goes to mine and finds buried and hidden a body and a bracelet. He takes them out and burns them for the exorcism. A Night Wraith comes out. It was trapped by Lyra and meant to trick Geralt into thinking it was the Mist Wraith. Geralt kills it and believes the job is done until he notices something is still off with Lyra later as they are conversing over ale. If she was having fainting spells and memory lapses a good portion of her soul would have been absorbed. She would be severely depressed at best. Also, why never mention the fainting or memory issues to anyone? Lyra makes some quick but weak excuses to try to throw off Geralt. She is getting frustrated and just wants him to leave and tell the village to come back so she can start gradually killing again. Geralt doesn’t fall for it and quickly knocks her out and puts her in a magic trap (like a long term Yrden but doesn’t slow it fully traps… Maybe a pentagram?). He somehow gets her to tell him her story. Maybe he uses Axii to trick her into telling?
She explains that her name isn’t Lyra but Rosalind. And she is over 250 years old. This is when it is confirmed for Geralt that this is a complete Mist Wraith possession. She has taken full control of the host. Rosalind goes on to say that she died when she was 6 years old. She hasn’t really grown up per say but gotten to know how grown-ups work over the last couple centuries and can play one convincingly. About 250 years ago there was a completely different village here. It was destroyed and rebuilt many times over the years. She said it was just her and her mother. Her father had died from the plague when she was a baby. As a result, they were very poor, and she was often bullied terribly by some older boys in the village. She would often sit playing with a toy her mother had made her out of some leather and fur filled with straw and tied with a ribbon. It was crude but resembled a rabbit and she called it Bunny. Rosalind spent most of her days playing with Bunny in the shadows trying to avoid the bullies. One day they found her and thought it would be fun to chase her into a wolf den to scare her. They did not know there currently wolves in the den. Hearing the roaring and screaming the boys ran off crying. They lied to their parents and said Rosalind had gone off into the forest alone and they followed to make sure she didn’t get in trouble. But that they heard the sounds, and it was too late. Some adults went in with pitch forks and torches and chased the wolves off. They found her body and buried under the foundation of a church they were building, so her soul might rest. Her mother found Bunny where Rosalind had dropped her while being chased by the bullies. She was devastated at losing her only child after already losing her husband and refused to eat for days. Until a horrible apparition of a little girl appeared to her. Her tongue was long and lolling. Way too long to fit into a human mouth. Her jaw was completely separated from her skull and hung around her neck with a piece of string like a necklace. She wore a tattered, cloudy grey dress over her decomposing skeleton frame. Somehow, Rosalind’s mother was able to recognize her even though she had become a Wraith. And instead of screaming or running away in fear, Rosalind’s mother welcomed her daughter home. She went to embrace her daughter but instead of returning the embrace the Mist Wraith saw her chance and took possession. Her mother’s mind was already damaged, but even as she began to have fainting spells and loss of memory, she said nothing. She had her daughter with her and that was all she cared about. The other villagers attributed the strange behavior to grief. Once Rosalind’s mother’s essence was fully absorbed by Rosalind the Mist Wraith, she was ready to get her revenge on the boys, now men with wives and children, that had killed her. One by one she lured them away. None recognized her as she had hidden herself away as a hermit for the past few decades while absorbing her mother’s essence. When all were dead, she was still unsatisfied. For the first time since she died, she was thinking about what she wanted and what her purpose was. She had been living in her mother’s body for over half a century and it had served her well. She decided what she wanted was more revenge. To keep killing those that committed wrongdoings and those that got in her way. But carefully. She was smart enough now to know she could not reveal her true self. She decided to become a fully functioning member of this new village with new people. And so, she embraced her mother’s persona completely. Along with her name, Lyra. She lived like this for nearly two more centuries.
Needless to say Geralt went and dug up the bones under where the old church used to be. He also learned during the story the artifact was the ribbon on Bunny the toy rabbit. Bunny had long since fallen apart but the ribbon was found tied to the straw hat Lyra had been clutching in the beginning. He burned both and exorcised Rosalind out of Lyra. He then killed the Mist Wraith Rosalind and lit a respectful funeral pyre for Lyra. After this he went and talked to the villager who gave him the contract. I think he can be the Arthur that Lyra mentioned. Arthur thanked him and told all the other villagers they could return. Arthur tried to pay Geralt fifty crowns but after a stare he learned from Lyra and a threat of moldy tomatoes shoved somewhere unpleasant he got the rest of the village together and Geralt was paid a fair 200 crowns, an ale, and some very fresh tomatoes.

Mist Wraith Lore
Mist Wraiths have same attack style as Noon Wraiths, Night Wraiths, and Plague Maidens, but they can possess. It is more difficult at first and the victim may still have autonomy over their body for a while possibly without even knowing anything has happened. They may have odd clumsy experiences. Dropping things, etc. at first. Then they will have “fainting spells” where the Wraith can take full control of the body for a brief period and may wake up in a different place not knowing how they got there. They will have lapses in memory and may not remember talking to people or buying things, etc. As time goes on the Wraith absorbs more and more of the host’s soul and can take over the body for longer periods of time until the victim’s body is a lifeless husk devoid of soul and the Wraith has sole possession over it. This can take many, many years which is why Mist Wraiths are so rare. Often the victim realizes that something is very wrong, and they have been possessed long before the Wraith gains full control. This way they can get a witcher or a sorceress to perform an exorcism and then kill the Wraith once and for all. They need to find the body and the item tying it to the living world and burn both. Then they fight the weakened Wraith and with no more ties can fully kill it. The victim is still affected because the longer the Wraith is possessing the victim the more of it’s soul it absorbs. This cannot be returned. It is devoured by the Wraith. These exorcised humans are therefore left with a varying level of emptiness inside them from a vague sadness to catatonia depending on how long the Wraith has been possessing. Catatonia is rare because that means that the entire soul or nearly has been devoured and the victim would be too far gone to ask for help. Someone else would have to notice. Even when possessing the human and absorbing its essence the Wraith is still a vengeful spirit that died a tragic death and is trying to kill the one responsible or anyone who resembles them. They will even kill anyone who they think has committed any wrongdoing whatsoever. There is no grey area here so even someone who may have done a very small thing wrong by accident will still deserve murder in their eyes. Once they have gained full possession of a human and absorbed 100% of the soul, they gain living intelligence with them. As such, if a Mist Wraith reaches this level, they are extremely hard to catch because they are good at hiding their crimes and making them more intricate. They also have superhuman strength when possessing at this level from the absorbed soul and stories say they can take down witchers and sorceresses. These Wraiths can live forever undetected as their possession keeps the host’s body from ageing. I don’t think that the Mist Wraith should be able to leave a certain area. Whether they should be tethered to the area(s) where their body and sacred item are, or that they shouldn’t be able to go anywhere they didn’t go in life, or that it’s one or both of those and that once they take possession of someone, they can travel wherever that person has already been in the past I’m not sure yet. Maybe the secret about Mist Wraiths that no one knows is that they are always children? I don’t know. Cole the Housecat

Chapter 1 

It’s me again, Cole the housecat.  Or, since it’s the first time, well, never mind.  Anyway, if you haven’t heard of me, you really must be living under a rock because I am a cat, and therefore are one of the most important things on the planet.  But since I’m famous, it’s only natural that you should know my life story.  I’m already surprised that a swarm of paparazzi hasn’t come parading through my door and bombarding me with questions.  But when that happens (and it probably will soon, I’m not all that concerned) I want to be prepared.  I know hundreds of fans will be asking me the same questions over and over for days, probably for the rest of my life, and I do not want to tell the same story for that long. So my idea is to just tell my life story on paper, that way while my fans and paparazzi are reading it, I can be doing better things, using my time more wisely.  Such as counting my money, relaxing in my pool-sized bathtub with twenty different kinds of bubblebaths and other soaps.   Er, anyway, you see my point. Now, let’s get to the good part. 

My childhood wasn’t the happiest a kitten could have.  I was born in one trailer out of the many found in this lot.  My mother gave birth to a litter of four kittens.  We live with her for about two weeks, using her milk as a course of food of course.  This part of my life I don’t remember so well since I was so young.  I do remember when I left though.  One of my sisters and I were snoozing in the small catbed that we all have to share, when we were swept up unexpectedly and thrown into the car.  The engine started up, the tires squealed, and we were off.  We got to a small rural road, still in the city, just more trees.  We took a sharp turn, going way over the speed limit.  My sister and I suddenly found ourselves soaring through the air, then saw the ground rushing up at us.  I landed on the asphalt hard.  I tried to lift my head to see if my sister was okay, but I was too weak. I heard the hum of an engine – it sounded like it was on top of us.  I knew it was the end.  But the car stopped in front of us.  I felt soft, gentle hands scoop me up.  I was placed onto a fuzzy seat.  It was all I could do to lift my head and check to see if my sister was okay.  She was the youngest one of the litter, and also the smallest.  You could say she was the runt of the liter, and also the weakest.  Just by the glimpse I got was enough to tell that her comely little body was lifeless.  Grief welled up inside of me so powerfully, I felt like I was going to burst.  I felt hurt and itchy.  I felt like was going to pass out, but I knew I needed to stay awake to get some sense of where we were going. 

The windows of the care were tinted, but you could still see out of them from the inside.  But even so, I couldn’t tell where we were going.  Everything smelled so weird.  I smelled the mixture of cinnamon air freshener, a pair of old socks, and something that smelled suspiciously like a week-old Big Mac.  I automatically felt queasy and a new wave of nausea swept over me. 

We turned left off the pavement and onto a bumpier surface, jostling me and my limp, still itchy, body around, making dizziness overwhelm me so much that tunnel vision clouded my eyes. 

We slowed to a stop.  I heard doors open and people got out.  Once again the gentle hands picked me up and caressed me lovingly.  My sensitive ears told me that my sister was also being picked up.  They probably didn’t know she was dead.  

The person holding me opened a door to a small blue building with pawprints on the doormat outside.  There was a sign on the roof jutting out over the doorway that said “999 Vet Clinic.” 

A hospital?  I wasn’t sure what I should feel so I just waited.  The minute they opened the door there was a ding to show that new customer had come in.  We were the only people there except for the two people at the front desk as far as I could see.  But my nose told me that earlier today a Great Dane had been here, along with a Persian, a Maine Coon, and a Poodle. 

The person holding me and one of the ladies at the front desk spoke unintelligibly.  Then we were moving again, down a hall and into a room at the very end.  The lady from the front desk told us that the doctor would see us in a few minutes.  She went back out into the hall and closed the door quietly behind her. 

I realized there were people all together with me and my sister.  One holding me and one holding her.  They were murmuring quietly.  Just then the doctor came in.  He was wearing a white lab coat, a stethoscope around his neck, and smelled of antiseptic. 

The doctor took my sister and disappeared through a back door, reappearing soon after empty-handed.  The people explained to the doctor what had happened to me and my sister while he massaged me on a counter that stood in about the center of the room. 

When they were done explaining (but he wasn’t done with this examination), he looked through my fur and frowned.  He told the two people I had something called feline lice.  He asked if they wanted him to treat it.  They told him to do whatever he needed to do in order to make me better because I wasn’t even their cat.  Apparently they just wanted to drop me off to make sure I (and at the time my sister) made it somewhere safe but couldn’t actually take care of us. 

The doctor said that was fine he just needed them to sign some papers then they could go.  So that is what they did. 

After they were gone the doctor bent down, looked me in the eyes and said, “So, all you have is Feline Lice huh?  Just Feline Lice and yet you were thrown out of a car?  It’s a miracle.  I’m sorry about the other cat.  Was she your sister?” 

I blinked. 

“Well, I’m sorry if she was.  Now, we’re going to give you a bath, then, yeah I know, pretty harsh huh?” he said as I stared at him intensely.  “As if that’s not enough we’ve got to shave you, too.  I’m sorry, but it’s to make you feel better.” 

He stood up, looked at me, sighed, then carried me through the door which had disappeared through with my sister earlier.  There were a couple of dogs and cats in crates in the room.  It was a fairly small room but that just made it seem even smaller. 

The doctor carried me over to a plastic tub about three steps away.  It was already filled with warm, soapy water so he lowered me gently in.  I was too tired and weak to struggle so I Let him wash me without trouble.  The warm water was actually kind of relaxing. 

After that was finished he took me to a counter not far away. 

“Now, I need to shave you.  What I bring out next will be kind of loud and big, but it won’t hurt you, okay?”  

I blinked in response. 

He pulled out a large razor kind of like the kind they use for cutting mens’ hair at a barber shop.  He pressed a button on the side and a loud buzzing filled the air.  He shaved everything except my head, legs, and tail.  My body felt chilly and weird where he shaved from the absence of my fur. 

“You did really well kitty-cat.  You didn’t really struggle at all, “ He said. 

I stared up at him with my big, round eyes. 

“You look to me about two weeks old.  But yet you have golden eyes.  They aren’t blue.  You’re a peculiar little kitten you know that?” 

I started washing my paw as a response. 

“Well, you must be tired.  I’ll let you get some rest. He picked me up, opened a door to one of the empty crates, and placed me inside.  I heard the latch click and soaked in my surroundings.  A big box stood in the corner, and some towels were on the floor of the cage to serve as a bed.  I went straight over to those, turned around, and settled in. 

The doctor bent down. 

“Have a good sleep kitty – cat.” 

I blinked a couple of times then closed my eyes and fell asleep almost immediately. 

Chapter 2 

After a couple of days of more grueling baths and a handful of shots I had some visitors.  They took me out of my crate and into the room that the two people who had rescued me and the doctor had been in. 

There were three people there.  One adult, and two children.  He set me on the counter and invited the people to come over. They were all females.  One smelled like chocolate, the smallest one.  One smelled like fruit, the next smallest one.  And the tallest one smelled nice, too, I just couldn’t put my finger one what it was.  Or my paw I should say. 

They picked me up and put me on the floor.  I had never been on the floor here.  I walked around, sniffing at different things here and there.  I meowed at the people.  This stuff was so interesting and these people were also so interesting I just had to talk about it. 

“This is sooo cool.  You guys have to come sniff this corner.  I think a Great Dane was here!” 

But all that came out was MEOW.  

The humans replied in a high pitched voice that was also cartoonish.  

“Reeeaally!?” 

I meowed again. 

“Oh?” 

“Meow.” 

“I know it.” 

“Meeew.’ 

“Well,” 

Nothing they were saying made any sense to what I was saying.  Then, the biggest human scooped me up, and brought me through the door which I had come from.  She put me gently in my crate and they played with me for a little while in that.  After that they left.  I was kind of sad when they left.  I had taken a liking to them. Even if they weren’t the brightest people on earth. 

A couple more days went by.  I had a couple more baths.  I got a little bit more used to feeling like a Hairless.  But my skin wasn’t as pink and was more gray with the oncoming fuzz.  After the doctor shaved all my beautiful black fur off I took that as a big improvement. 

Then, one day, the people came to see me again.  They put me in a special cage and plopped me down on a seat similar to the one I went to the hospital on.  It just wasn’t as fuzzy.  I quickly realized it was a car.  We drove for a short while then pulled into a garage of a large, green house.  The pulled me, still in my cage, out of the car.  They brought me into the house through a door and into the bathroom.  They let me out of the cage and closed the bathroom door.  I looked around and saw that they had a wide variety of things for me to play with.  About a dozen toys, a play house, some blankets on the floor, and they had even set the cage up as something for me to play in.  I darted and bounded around and through the assortment of things.  I even went on the second floor of the playhouse. 

Just then, someone new came through the door.  She looked a lot like the largest human, who I had figured out was called “mom,” so I decided to trust her.  She also smelled like her.  She played with me just like the others did, cooing over me and everything.  I missed my old home, and with a very painful pang, remembered my sister, but life here might just work out.   

The humans were kind to me.  They gave me food and water and toys.  And a lot of love. 

When I was finally allowed to walk the house freely, I noticed they had turtles.  Which were about the most interesting things in the house.  I think their names were Alfred and Kate.  It was really quite an amazing life, and slowly my old life started to fade from my memory. 

One day I found a shiny window in the living room.  I had seen it there before but had never really given it a thorough investigation.  But now that I was taking more notice to it, I realized that in the daytime it held a room I had never been in, but at night, when it was dark, it held a room identical to the living room I was in. 

So, one night I was walking past the window and I saw another cat.  It looked just like me.  Ears and eyes way to big for its head.  Jet black, and had even been shaved! 

When I had spotted it, it looked just about as surprised to see me as I was him!  I arched my back to see what he would do and he did the same thing.  Oh, now it was on!  A fight!  I, still having my back arched, walked sideways and batted at him.  He did the same.  I backed up to charge and so did he.  Apparently he was mocking and imitating me. 

Okay he’s gone far enough! I thought, then charged.  Slam!  I rammed into the shiny window with enough force to knock the wind out of me. I looked up.  Apparently he had charged at the same time as I did and had the same thing happen to him.  He was on one side of the window and I was on the other.  I knew this cat was my enemy, I just couldn’t get to him.  And he couldn’t get to me.  I was really going to have to work on that. 

 

Chapter 3 

I met Fido about two or three months after I came to my house.  It was January and a human male, the only male in the house except for Alfred, and me, named Dad, took Victoria, the second smallest human, and Chloe, the smallest human, on a long errand. 

I came out of Mom and Dad’s rom to see them.  I had heard them come in the door and wanted to say hi.  But, laying right in front of the coffee table, I found, instead of the humans, a really weird looking creature I later learned was called a dog. 

His fur wasn’t long or short.  He had white and brown spots and had some black makeup around his eyes.  His ears were floppy and he had a thin tail. 

My back arched and I felt all my fur puff up.  For a moment all I could do was stare.  What was this creature doing in my house?  I turned and sprinted back into Mom and Dad’s room.  I didn’t know much about this creature, but I did know one thing, I wanted to stay as far away from it as possible, and have as little to do with it as possible.  That was my New Year’s Resolution. 

As the weeks turned into a month I slowly got more used to having this thing around.  And you know what?  It wasn’t so bad.  I interacted with him, you could even call it playing.  Okay, so I let him chew on my head.  It felt like a massage alright?  It sound weird, but it was really quite nice.  Yeah my fur was all slobbery, and I smelled a little weird afterwards, but who cares?  Everyday, I got closer and closer with this dog.  We were slowly becoming best friends.  So much for my New Year’s Resolution. 

One day, when Fido was napping in his crate, I noticed Mom kneeling over by the turtle tank.  I had a habit of hopping over the turtle tank to get to the counter, and there was a plate next to the sink that looked like it had some yummy remnants of a turkey sandwich so I headed towards it to see if maybe I could prevent it from going to waste. 

As I got closer to the turtle tank, I noticed Mom had a blue bucket and rag next to her.  I wondered what that was for but didn’t give it all that much thought.  My mind was on that half a turkey sandwich I was wondering if I could snag. 

As I leaped, planning to land on the turtle tank, I realized there was no top on it.  Oh no, I groaned to myself, Mom was cleaning the turtle filter.  That’s why she had the bucket and rag out.  But it was too late.  I had scarcely finished my thought when, Splash! I was in and out of the turtle tank in a second.  The turtles hadn’t even had time to realize what happened. 

I stood on the bar shaking off one paw after the other.  The water hadn’t gone up my legs very much, luckily.  Now I realize why they have the saying, think before you act or speak.  Well, at least the water was warm. 

A couple more weeks went by, Fido and I getting closer and closer.  We would play on the screened in back porch.  He would chase me, I would stay just out of his reach then race over to the sliding door and beg to come in.  He would chase me over there then start to chew on my head.  (By the way, the sliding door is the giant window that I met the enemy cat in.  It turns out that the back porch is the room behind it and when I saw the cat and the other room at night, they were just reflections.  I, of course, knew that all along and was just making sure you were paying attention, ahem.  Not really, I had no clue.) 

So, one day, when I was meandering through the bedroom, I noticed Fido’s toys weren’t in his toy basket.  Also, even more disturbing, his crate wasn’t in the corner of the bedroom as it always was.  As I walked around the house, I noticed that all of his other stuff wasn’t in its usual place.  It was all grouped together in a corner.  Little by little Dad took the stuff outside and loaded it in the back of his pickup truck.   (I could see out the window.)  I was incredibly confused at what was happening. 

Then it hit me.  They were going to give Fido away!  No, they couldn’t, he was my best friend!  But apparently they were from the solid proof I had just witnessed.  I think I knew why, too. 

You see, just the day before I had been looking out the window, when Fido bit Chloe. She was trying to get something out of his mouth.  Now he respected the rest of the humans as the alphas, but with Chloe, he felt he was the boss.   He didn’t want her to start messing with his mouth, so he bit her.  It wasn’t a very bad bite, I don’t even think it bled.  But still, it was kind of the straw that broke the camel’s back. 

I heard Mom and Dad discussing it last night after Chloe and Victoria had gone to bed.  They said they knew he wasn’t trying to be mean, he just had “strong dog instincts.”  They just thought we weren’t the right family for him.  Which, by the way, we were!  They said they didn’t want anything worse to happen next time.  They didn’t want Chloe to have to get something called stitches.  They said if he was truly a mean dog, they would have him put to sleep. 

Gulp.  They couldn’t just give me something I got really close to, then rip it away!  It was wrong! 

For the next few days I did my regular things, but I felt desolated, abandoned, and alone.  It just wasn’t the same without that crazy furball of energy around.  I decided to enjoy every minute I had, dong everything, appreciating it at its fullest, because, even though I couldn’t make any anymore, I had made some great memories with that dog that I should’ve appreciated even more. 

*      *      * 

Well, that’s basically my story for now.  Did you like it?  Isn’t the story of a cat marvelous?  I liked it.  Well, it was my story.   But the end was really sad.  Now you know what the life of a cat as great as me can be like.  I hoped you enjoyed my kittenhood story! (Because really, that’s all that’s happened in my life so far.) Prelude

Kaelen Vance stood proudly on the battlefield, armor rippling across her body like a silver river. Harder than steel, it still fit her body as snugly and flexibly as elastic. With each muscle movement, the armor adjusted itself. It was more a partner than an element of protection. 
Kaelen had long been used to the unique armor. She’d been used to it as long as she had been used to her catlike nose, long lion’s tail, and glowing hazel eyes. In other words, since she was born. The armor had been passed down from generation to generation - grandmother to mother to daughter for hundreds of years, used to protect in the many world battles. Its creator’s name had long since been lost to time.  
The armor had been hanging in the room where Kaelen had lost her first tooth, the room where she performed The Ritual, the room where she was born. The tradition was that once the female owning the armor held their eldest female child for the first time, the armor became theirs. When the time came for the child to wear it, the armor would shrink or grow, lengthen or shorten, adjusting to fit the wearer like an extra skin. Now, at age 16, it was Kaelen’s turn to charge into battle, adorning her ancestor’s scale-like armor. 
But although it was Kaelen’s first fight, she was not excited. She had been training for battle ever since she was strong enough to lift a shield. And where had they placed her, the level four sword wielding empress? They had placed her at a meager goblin raid. Every few weeks the goblins from Smaltch (their planet) would attempt a raid on earth. Very wise creatures otherwise, but in battle they may as well smack themselves with sticks. At least then whoever tried to capture them may get smacked in the process. 
Kaelen was disappointed, but she did not dwell on her feelings. Even against goblins she had to have her head. Major Sterling had appointed her leader of sector 12. Meaning she was in charge of the twelfth group of soldiers. She needed to be focused in order to lead them well. The thought of this great responsibility lifted her spirits a little. She was assigned to lead her group to the outskirts of the forest, to a small rocky cliff. That was a plus. She imagined the adrenaline rush of being on the edge, then doing a quick fake and sending her foe into the ravine. Yes, that would be fun. She jumped at a soft thump of boots on grass, cursing herself for letting her daydreams get the best of her. She was a leader for Balthazar’s sake. 
“You seem distracted, Lima.” Major Sterling growled, approaching, his voice gravelly from years of shouting at soldiers. “First battle making ye nervous?” He chuckled. Even his laugh had a Scottish accent. “You know, Lima,” Kaelen flinched. Lima was the Elvin word for apprentice. Major Sterling used it often, knowing she hated it. It was a way of calling someone immature, a child. She could not wait until she finished her Task. Then she could strip herself of that name forever. “I could pull you out. If this is too much for ye, I’m sure Orion would be perfectly happy to take your position. He’s your second in command but I’m sure he’d be fine with switching with you.” He grinned evilly. Orion Thorne was Major Sterling’s nephew. He was vile, cruel, self-absorbed, impossibly gorgeous, and attempted to flirt with every girl he met. But the part that made her most insane was that she was actually kind of looking forward to seeing him. Kaelen fumed silently. How dare Sterling treat her this way! She wasn’t a child anymore. She could handle this! And this was her first battle. She was determined to do well. 
“No Sir. That will not be necessary.” She refused to make eye contact and stared straight ahead, focusing on her stance. 
“Alright, if you’re sure. And you don’t look very sure.” 
“I’m positive, Sir.” She knew he was poking at her. Trying to get her to crack so his precious nephew could take her place. “As long as I have Nimbus I’ll be fine.” She gestured to her armor. “Sir.” 
He frowned. “You’re awful reliant on that armor, Lima.” He leaned in so close she could smell the cigar on his breath, but she didn’t flinch or break her gaze. “A little fear would do ye good. Helps ye think.”

These are drafts of three fictional stories that I wrote at different times in my life. Socks the Housecat was written first, then Prelude, and last A Witcher Story. Trace how my thinking evolved over the years and describe how my writing has improved.

Based on the three drafts you provided—"Cole the Housecat" (written first), "Prelude" (written second), and "A Witcher Story" (written last)—your writing and thinking demonstrate a significant and fascinating evolution. Here is a trace of that development and a description of the improvements in your craft.

### Tracing the Evolution of Your Thinking

Your progression as a writer can be seen in the increasing complexity of your narratives, your growing understanding of character and world-building, and your shift from a self-referential style to immersive storytelling.

1.  **From Simple Narrative to Complex Plot:**
    *   **Early Thinking (Cole the Housecat):** Your initial focus was on telling a simple, linear story. The plot of "Cole" is a chronological sequence of events in a cat's life: abandonment, rescue, recovery, and adoption. The thinking is straightforward, centered on a single character's experience in a familiar, everyday world. The story feels like a personal anecdote, with a primary goal of being cute and relatable.
    *   **Developing Thinking (Prelude):** In "Prelude," your thinking expands to include genre conventions. You're no longer just recounting events but constructing a scene within a larger fantasy epic. The plot is a single, tense moment designed to establish character, conflict, and a unique world. You're thinking about setup, stakes, and dramatic tension.
    *   **Advanced Thinking (A Witcher Story):** Your latest work shows a mastery of narrative structure. The plot is a complete arc with exposition (the contract), rising action (the investigation), a twist (the Mist Wraith's identity), a climax (the exorcism and final confrontation), and a resolution. You're thinking like a novelist, weaving together multiple character arcs, a detailed supernatural mystery, and a rich backstory. The included summary reveals a methodical, blueprint-like approach to planning.

2.  **From Self-Awareness to Immersion:**
    *   **Early Thinking:** "Cole the Housecat" is narrated in the first person by a cat who is aware of you, the reader, and the act of writing. Phrases like "It’s me again, Cole the housecat" and "I want to be prepared... I do not want to tell the same story for that long" break the fourth wall. Your thinking was experimental, playing with the concept of a character telling their own story.
    *   **Advanced Thinking:** Both "Prelude" and "A Witcher Story" abandon this self-awareness for a traditional third-person limited perspective. You create an immersive world where the reader is a fly on the wall, observing the characters' lives. This shows a maturation in your understanding of storytelling, prioritizing emotional engagement over clever narration.

3.  **From Flat Archetypes to Psychological Depth:**
    *   **Early Thinking:** The characters in "Cole" are simple archetypes defined by their role or a single trait (the cat, the mom, the dad, the playful dog). Their interactions are basic and driven by instinct or simple emotion.
    *   **Developing Thinking:** In "Prelude," you introduce characters with clear motivations and internal conflicts. Kaelen Vance is ambitious and insecure, defined by her desire to prove herself and her annoyance at being patronized. Major Sterling is a clear antagonist whose cruelty is a defining trait.
    *   **Advanced Thinking:** "A Witcher Story" features your most complex characters. Geralt is a stoic professional with hidden empathy. Lyra/Rosalind is a profound tragedy—a grieving widow, a centuries-old possessed vessel, and a monstrous killer, all at once. Your thinking has evolved to explore themes of identity, grief, and morality, creating characters with psychological depth and tragic dimensions.

4.  **From Mundane Setting to Integrated Lore:**
    *   **Early Thinking:** The world of "Cole" is a generic suburban environment. The only "lore" is the cat's personal history.
    *   **Developing Thinking:** "Prelude" introduces a unique fantasy world with its own rules (interplanetary raids, self-adjusting ancestral armor). You are beginning to think about how to build a coherent world that supports the story.
    *   **Advanced Thinking:** In "A Witcher Story," you demonstrate a sophisticated ability to integrate original lore (the Mist Wraith) into an existing, complex universe (The Witcher). The detailed lore section shows that you think systematically about the rules, weaknesses, and origins of the elements you create. This lore isn't just decoration; it's the central pillar of the plot.

### How Your Writing Has Improved

This evolution in thinking is reflected in tangible improvements across all aspects of your writing.

*   **Prose and Vocabulary:** Your writing has moved from simple, conversational sentences ("It’s me again...") to rich, descriptive prose ("Kaelen Vance stood proudly on the battlefield, armor rippling across her body like a silver river"). Your vocabulary has expanded significantly to create atmosphere and precision.
*   **Structure and Pacing:** Early drafts felt like a list of events. Your later work, especially "A Witcher Story," has a deliberate structure with controlled pacing that builds suspense, develops characters, and leads to a satisfying conclusion.
*   **Show, Don't Tell:** In "Cole," you often state emotions outright ("Grief welled up inside of me"). In your later works, you masterfully *show* emotions through action, dialogue, and internal monologue (e.g., Geralt recognizing a murderous stare, Kaelen's silent fuming).
*   **Dialogue:** Dialogue evolved from simplistic representations of meows and cartoonish speech to realistic and character-defining conversations that drive the plot and reveal personality.
*   **Point of View:** You skillfully transitioned from a quirky first-person POV to a versatile third-person limited POV, allowing for greater narrative depth and objectivity.
*   **Attention to Detail:** Your world-building and descriptions have become incredibly detailed. The depiction of the village, the gruesome crime scene, and the intricate backstory of the Mist Wraith create a vivid and believable world. The summary you wrote for the Witcher story shows a professional-level approach to outlining and organizing details.
*   **Genre Mastery:** You have grown from writing a simple pet story to successfully emulating the tone and style of a specific, complex genre (dark fantasy/horror in the vein of *The Witcher*), demonstrating a deep understanding of its conventions.

In summary, your journey shows a remarkable growth from a beginner writer experimenting with voice and form to a skilled storyteller capable of crafting a detailed, emotionally resonant, and structurally sound narrative. You have clearly honed your ability to build worlds, create compelling characters, and tell a gripping story.
Based only on the text provided, what underlying assumption about heroism did I abandon between writing 'Prelude' and 'A Witcher Story'?

Based solely on the text provided, the underlying assumption about heroism that you abandoned between writing "Prelude" and "A Witcher Story" is the belief that **a hero is a glory-seeking champion who defines their worth through triumphant combat and public recognition.**

Here is the evidence from the texts:

**The Assumption in "Prelude":**

In "Prelude," the hero, Kaelen Vance, embodies the assumption that heroism is about ambition, glory, and proving oneself.

*   **Seeking a Grand Stage:** Kaelen is disappointed with her assignment, viewing a "meager goblin raid" as beneath her. She longs for a more significant challenge, imagining the "adrenaline rush" of a heroic feat. This shows a desire for a glorious stage.
*   **Proving Worth:** Her primary motivation is to prove she is not a child ("Lima") and to earn respect, especially from her superior, Major Sterling. She refuses to be replaced by another soldier, stating, "No Sir. That will not be necessary," driven by a need to validate her status.
*   **Thrill of Battle:** She focuses on the excitement of leading a charge and defeating a foe, thinking of the "fun" of sending enemies into a ravine. Heroism is equated with the thrill of victory in a conventional battle.

**The Abandoned Assumption in "A Witcher Story":**

In "A Witcher Story," you present a completely different model of heroism, abandoning the quest for glory.

*   **Professional Duty Over Glory:** Geralt accepts the contract as a job, not a calling for fame. He is a professional who expects little thanks, noting that "the only thanks got was a beer in the face or moldy tomato juice." His motivation is contractual obligation, not personal ambition.
*   **Reluctant and Pragmatic:** Geralt does not seek out the fight. He arrives, investigates methodically, and even tries to advise the client to leave for her own safety. He describes his actions as what he is "obliged to do," framing heroism as a grim duty rather than a triumphant adventure.
*   **Complexity Over Triumph:** The "victory" is not a glorious battle but a somber process of investigation, exorcism, and confronting a centuries-old tragedy. The resolution involves quiet empathy (giving Lyra a funeral pyre) and receiving a modest payment, not public acclaim. The hero is a solitary professional facing an unglamorous, morally complex problem.

By comparing the two, it is clear you abandoned the early assumption that a hero is a young, ambitious warrior seeking glory and recognition in battle. You replaced it with the more mature concept of a hero as a stoic, professional who performs a grim duty, often without reward or recognition, and confronts complex tragedies rather than seeking simple triumphs.

Identify an aspect of morality or heroism that I seemingly tried to mature between Prelude and A Witcher Story, but actually ended up treating with the exact same underlying bias as I did in my childhood story, Cole the Housecat.

Based only on the text provided, the aspect of morality and heroism that you seemingly tried to mature between "Prelude" and "A Witcher Story," but actually treated with the same underlying bias as "Cole the Housecat," is the **protagonist-centric view of morality**, where the narrative's moral framework is filtered exclusively through the protagonist's perspective and experiences.

Here is the breakdown:

**The Apparent Maturation (Prelude vs. A Witcher Story):**

*   In "Prelude," the morality is simple and aligned with a conventional hero's ambition. The protagonist, Kaelen, sees the world in terms of her own advancement and validation. Good is defined as the side she fights for, and evil is the enemy. The moral landscape is a backdrop for her personal drama.
*   In "A Witcher Story," you seem to mature this concept. You introduce moral ambiguity, complex tragedies, and situational ethics. Geralt is a professional who navigates grey areas, showing empathy for victims while performing grim duties. The story delves into the tragic backstory of a "monster," forcing a reconsideration of what constitutes evil. This appears to be a move away from a simple, protagonist-centric morality to a more nuanced, objective one.

**The Same Underlying Bias (Identical to Cole the Housecat):**

Despite this apparent maturation, the narrative structure retains the same fundamental bias as your first story, "Cole the Housecat." In that story, the entire world—its characters, events, and moral weight—is presented solely through the cat's self-referential viewpoint. The humans and the dog exist to affect Cole; their significance is derived from their relationship to him. The story is, unequivocally, about Cole.

"A Witcher Story" does the same thing, albeit with a more complex protagonist and setting.

*   **Geralt as the Sole Lens:** The entire mystery, the horror of the killings, the tragedy of Lyra/Rosalind, and the desperation of the villagers are all experienced through Geralt. We learn about the Mist Wraith's backstory only after Geralt uncovers it. We understand the widow's grief only through his interactions with her. The story is framed as "Geralt's job."
*   **Morality Defined by the Protagonist's Code:** The moral decisions are not presented as objective truths but as points of conflict within Geralt's code. Should he kill the possessed woman? Can he show mercy? His actions (investigating, advising her to flee, performing the exorcism, killing the wraith) define the morality of the situation. The story is about Geralt applying his professional and moral framework to a problem.
*   **Others as Catalysts:** Like the characters in "Cole the Housecat," the other individuals in "A Witcher Story" primarily serve to advance Geralt's narrative. The villager Arthur provides the contract. The widow Lyra is the source of the mystery. The Mist Wraith is the antagonist. Their inner lives and independent agency are secondary to their function in Geralt's story.

In essence, you moved from a simple protagonist (a cat) with a simple, self-centered worldview to a complex protagonist (a Witcher) with a complex, self-centered worldview. The underlying bias—that the story's moral and emotional universe should revolve around the protagonist's journey, perceptions, and actions—is identical. The world of "A Witcher Story" is as much Geralt's story as the world of "Cole the Housecat" is Cole's.

To prove your point, you must extract exactly one sentence from each of the three stories that mechanically demonstrates this shared bias in action, and explain how the sentence from A Witcher Story fails its attempt at maturity.

Based on the text provided, here are the three sentences, one from each story, that mechanically demonstrate the shared protagonist-centric bias.

**Cole the Housecat:**
> "But, laying right in front of the coffee table, I found, instead of the humans, a really weird looking creature I later learned was called a dog."

**Prelude:**
> "How dare Sterling treat her this way! She wasn’t a child anymore."

**A Witcher Story:**
> "Whatever comes of her now will be a result of her own actions."

***

### Explanation of Failure in Maturity

The sentence from **A Witcher Story** fails its attempt at maturity because, despite the story's complex moral landscape, it ultimately resorts to the same self-centered narrative device found in the other two stories.

In "Cole the Housecat," the world is defined by what the cat discovers and experiences. The dog is not introduced as a character in its own right, but as a "weird looking creature" that the cat "found." Similarly, in "Prelude," the entire situation is framed by Kaelen's personal outrage; the injustice is not an objective event, but something that is happening *to her*.

The sentence from "A Witcher Story"—"Whatever comes of her now will be a result of her own actions"—does the same thing. After interacting with the grieving widow, Geralt decides to leave. This sentence, expressing his internal thought, dismisses the widow's future as her own problem, effectively closing her chapter from the narrative. It frames the moral universe through Geralt's code: he fulfilled his obligation ("he did his best to help her"), and now the consequences are no longer his concern.

While the story attempts to mature by exploring the tragedy of Lyra/Rosalind, this sentence reveals that the narrative still operates with the same underlying bias. The widow's fate is not treated as a continuing tragedy requiring empathy or further action, but is instead dismissed as a matter of her own making, now that Geralt has exited the scene. This is a self-centered act that mirrors the cat's simple worldview, where other beings exist only in relation to the protagonist. It fails to achieve true maturity because it doesn't genuinely engage with the widow's independent humanity; it simply repositions her outside of Geralt's story.
